object-o.explain: を (said o) comes right after what the verb acts on, and the verb comes last: コーヒーを飲みます (coffee drink), 本を読みます (book read).
object-o.why: English shows what's drunk by putting it after the verb; Japanese marks it with を and keeps the verb for the end of the sentence.

examples.text: 私はコーヒーを飲みます。
お茶を飲みます。
私は牛乳とお水を飲みます。
本を読みます。

contrasts.says: English says drink coffee; Japanese says coffee を drink, the verb last.
は marks who the sentence is about; を what the verb acts on.

mistakes.wrong: コーヒーが飲みます。
mistakes.right: コーヒーを飲みます。
mistakes.why: What's drunk takes を: が never goes on it with 飲みます.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

question-ka.explain: か at the end of a sentence makes it a question; nothing else moves: 元気です (I'm well) → 元気ですか (are you well?). A question word sits where its answer would: どこですか (where is it?).
question-ka.why: English turns words around (Are you…? Do you…?); Japanese keeps the order and adds か, so the question is heard at the very end.

examples.text: 元気ですか。
食べますか。
コーヒーも飲みますか。
スマホはどこですか。

contrasts.says: English adds do or moves is to the front; Japanese adds か at the end.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

te-iru.explain: -ています says something is going on now: 読みます (I read) → 読んでいます (I'm reading); 飲みます → 飲んでいます.
te-iru.why: -ます alone says what you do, now or as a habit; -ています says it's going on right now, as English -ing does.

examples.text: 本を読んでいます。
何を飲んでいますか。
新聞を読んでいますか。
母は新聞を読んでいます。

contrasts.says: 読みます is what you do (I read); 読んでいます what's going on now (I'm reading).

mistakes.wrong: 本を読みでいます。
mistakes.right: 本を読んでいます。
mistakes.why: The form is 読んで, then います.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

topic-wa.explain: は (said wa) after a word makes it what the sentence is about: スマホは… (as for the phone…), 私は… (as for me…). What comes after says something about it.
topic-wa.why: English has no word for it: は sets the scene, and the rest of the sentence answers. It's written は but said wa.

examples.text: スマホはテーブルの上です。
examples.means: The phone is on the table.

examples.text: 車はどこですか。
私はお茶を飲みます。

contrasts.says: は says what you're talking about; が picks out who or what, often something new: 鍵があります.

mistakes.wrong: 私をお茶を飲みます。
mistakes.right: 私はお茶を飲みます。
mistakes.why: Who it's about takes は: を goes only on what's drunk.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

desu.explain: です after a noun or a place says what something is, or where: 車はここです (the car is here), 私の鍵です (it's my key). It's the same for I, you and it.
desu.why: English changes am, is and are; です never changes, and comes last.

examples.text: 車はここです。
これは私の鍵です。
はい、元気です。

contrasts.says: English has am, is and are; Japanese has です for all of them.

mistakes.wrong: 車はここだです。
mistakes.right: 車はここです。
mistakes.why: です alone; だ and です are the same word, plain and polite.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

adjectives.explain: A word like いい (good) takes です to be polite, as every い adjective does: いいです (it's good). 準備はいいですか (is the getting-ready good?) asks if you're ready.
adjectives.why: English needs is before an adjective; in Japanese the い word already says it, and です only makes it polite.

examples.text: 準備はいいですか。
はい、いいです。
はい、もういいです。
私はお茶がいいです。

contrasts.says: です after an い word makes it polite; after a noun it says what something is.

mistakes.wrong: 準備はいいだですか。
mistakes.right: 準備はいいですか。
mistakes.why: An い adjective takes です straight after it, never だ.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

possessive-no.explain: の joins two nouns, the owner first: 私の鍵 (my key), 友達のスマホ (my friend's phone), 母の車 (Mom's car). After an owner alone it means the one of: 私のです (it's mine).
possessive-no.why: English has my, your and 's; Japanese puts の after the owner for all of them.

examples.text: 私の鍵はここです。
友達のかばんは車の中です。
examples.means: My friend's bag is in the car.

examples.text: このスマホは私のです。

contrasts.says: English says my, your, Mom's; Japanese says 私の, 母の: the owner and の.

mistakes.wrong: スマホはテーブルに上です。
mistakes.right: スマホはテーブルの上です。
mistakes.why: 上 (on) is a noun: the table joins it with の, as an owner does.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

aru-iru.explain: あります says a thing is there, います a person or animal: テーブルの上にお茶があります (there's tea on the table), 母は車の中にいます (Mom is in the car). Where takes に.
aru-iru.why: English uses is for both; Japanese asks whether it's alive: あります for a key or tea, います for Mom or a friend.

examples.text: テーブルの上にお茶があります。
examples.literal: Table's top on tea is there.

examples.text: 母は車の中にいます。
かばんの中に鍵がありますか。
examples.means: Is there a key in the bag?
examples.literal: Bag's inside in key is there?

contrasts.says: English's is covers both; Japanese has あります for things, います for people and animals.

mistakes.wrong: テーブルの上にお茶がいます。
mistakes.right: テーブルの上にお茶があります。
mistakes.why: A thing is there with あります; います is for people and animals.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

particle-de.explain: で marks where you do something, に where you go: 家でお茶を飲みます (at home I drink tea); 家に帰ります (I go home).
particle-de.why: English uses at home and home for both; Japanese asks whether something is done there (で) or you go there (に).

examples.text: 家でお茶を飲みます。
家に帰ります。
母は家でコーヒーを飲みます。

contrasts.says: に is where you go, or where something is; で where something is done.

mistakes.wrong: 家を帰ります。
mistakes.right: 家に帰ります。
mistakes.why: Where you go takes に.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

masen.explain: -ません in place of -ます makes a verb not: 飲みます (drink) → 飲みません (don't drink), 帰ります → 帰りません. There's no do: the verb's ending says it.
masen.why: English adds do not; Japanese changes the ending of the verb itself.

examples.text: 私はコーヒーを飲みません。
まだ家に帰りません。
母は本を読みません。

contrasts.says: English adds don't or doesn't; Japanese changes -ます to -ません.

mistakes.wrong: コーヒーを飲むません。
mistakes.right: コーヒーを飲みません。
mistakes.why: The form is 飲みません.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

want-tai.explain: A verb's -ます part with たいです says what you want to do: 飲みます → 飲みたいです (I want to drink), 食べます → 食べたいです. What you want takes が or を.
want-tai.why: English says want to drink; Japanese adds たい to the verb itself, and です to stay polite.

examples.text: お茶が飲みたいです。
食べたいですか。

contrasts.says: -たいです is what you want; -ましょう invites someone to do it with you.

mistakes.wrong: お茶が飲むたいです。
mistakes.right: お茶が飲みたいです。
mistakes.why: たい goes on the -ます part: 飲み.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

masu.explain: -ます is the same for I, you, he and she: 私は飲みます, 母は飲みます, 友達は飲みます. Who does it comes from は, or isn't said at all.
masu.why: English adds -s for he and she; a Japanese verb never changes for who does it.

examples.text: 母はお茶を飲みます。
友達は本を読みます。
お茶を飲みます。

contrasts.says: English says I drink, she drinks; Japanese says 飲みます for both.

mistakes.wrong: 母は飲むます。
mistakes.right: 母は飲みます。
mistakes.why: The form is 飲みます.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

potential.explain: できます says can do: 何ができますか (what can I do?). A verb has a can form of its own: 手伝えます (can help), 読めます (can read). What you can takes が: 本が読めます.
potential.why: English adds can before the verb; Japanese changes the verb itself.

examples.text: 何ができますか。
母は手伝えます。
新聞が読めますか。

contrasts.says: English says can read; Japanese says 読めます, one word.

mistakes.wrong: 本が読めるます。
mistakes.right: 本が読めます。
mistakes.why: The form is 読めます.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

to-and.explain: と joins nouns: コーヒーとお茶 (coffee and tea). After a person it means with: 母と帰ります (I go home with Mom); 一緒に (together) often goes with it.
to-and.why: English has and and with; Japanese uses と for both, after the word it joins.

examples.text: コーヒーとお茶を飲みます。
母と帰ります。
私と一緒に帰りますか。
examples.means: Are you going home with me?

contrasts.says: English says with Mom; Japanese says 母と, と after the person.

mistakes.wrong: 母を帰ります。
mistakes.right: 母と帰ります。
mistakes.why: With someone takes と: を never goes with 帰ります.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

kosoado.explain: これ (this one) stands alone: これは私の鍵です. Before a noun it's この: この鍵 (this key). それ and その are that, near the one you're talking to.
kosoado.why: English's this works both ways; Japanese has これ on its own and この before a noun, and neither changes for the noun.

examples.text: これは私の鍵です。
この鍵は私のです。
このかばんは母のです。
それはだれのスマホですか。

contrasts.says: 私のです (it's mine) often follows: この鍵は私のです.

mistakes.wrong: このは私の鍵です。
mistakes.right: これは私の鍵です。
mistakes.why: Alone, it's これ; この needs a noun after it.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

subject-ga.explain: が marks what is there, or what you have, with あります: 仕事があります (work is there: I have work), 鍵があります (I have a key). With ありません, you don't.
subject-ga.why: English says I have; Japanese says the thing is there, marked with が.

examples.text: 仕事があります。
車がありますか。
仕事がありません。

contrasts.says: は is what you're talking about; が what's there, often new.

mistakes.wrong: 仕事をあります。
mistakes.right: 仕事があります。
mistakes.why: What there is takes が: を never goes with あります.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons, open to correction.

question-word.explain: だれ asks who, 何 what, どこ where, いつ when, and どうして why. Put the question word where the answer would go, and end with か. 予約は今日です becomes 予約はいつですか. When asking who does something, use だれが: だれが来ますか. 何 is なに before を here. The single words だれか and 何か mean someone and something, or anyone and anything in a question; their か does not make the whole sentence a question.
question-word.why: English often moves a question word to the front and adds do or changes the verb order. Japanese keeps the question word with the particle for its job. The verb or です still comes near the end, before the final か.

examples.text: だれが来ますか。
何を探していますか。
スマホはどこにありますか。
予約はいつですか。
どうしてですか。
そこに何かあります。

contrasts.says: 予約はいつですか keeps when after the appointment; English asks When is the appointment?
A question word asks for a missing detail. Sentence-final か makes the sentence a question; the か inside だれか or 何か instead makes an indefinite word.
だれが来ますか asks who is coming. が marks the unknown person as the subject.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

hoshii.explain: Put the thing you want before が欲しいです: お水が欲しいです. 欲しい is an い adjective, so です makes it polite. 少し can say how much: お水が少し欲しいです. A question such as お水が欲しいですか asks the listener about their wants. Said plainly, 欲しいです is about your own wants, or asks the person you're talking to about theirs; what someone else wants is said another way, later.
hoshii.why: English uses the verb want for things and actions. Japanese uses 欲しい for a thing and a verb with たい for an action.

examples.text: お水が少し欲しいです。
もう少しお水が欲しいです。
examples.means: I want a little more water.

examples.text: お水が欲しいですか。

contrasts.says: お水が欲しいです wants water; お水を飲みたいです wants to drink water.
The Japanese adjective follows what is wanted. English puts want first.

mistakes.wrong: お水が欲しいだです。
mistakes.right: お水が欲しいです。
mistakes.why: 欲しい takes です directly. Do not insert だ after an い adjective.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 41–60, open to correction.

adjective-negative.explain: For an い adjective, replace the final い with くない and keep です: 高いです becomes 高くないです, and 忙しいです becomes 忙しくないです; いい becomes よくないです. A な adjective keeps its word and takes じゃないです: 静かじゃないです. Both are everyday polite negatives. Having no money or time is different: お金がありません, 時間がありません. This rule does not make every word ending in い an い adjective.
adjective-negative.why: English adds not to is or am. Japanese changes the adjective’s ending, or uses the negative copula after a な adjective.

examples.text: このコーヒーは高くないです。
今日は忙しくないです。
この町は静かじゃないです。

contrasts.says: ありません says you do not have something. 忙しくないです says you are not busy.
高い changes to 高くない; 静か keeps its form before じゃないです.

mistakes.wrong: この町は静かじゃないだです。
mistakes.right: この町は静かじゃないです。
mistakes.why: The negative already ends in ない. Keep です directly after it, without だ.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 41–60, open to correction.

past-adjective.explain: An い adjective changes its final い to かった: 面白いです becomes 面白かったです, and いい becomes よかったです. The adjective itself says it was true in the past, while です remains the polite ending. A な adjective stays unchanged and uses でした: 静かでした. These lessons practice the affirmative past; other past forms come later.
past-adjective.why: English puts was or were before the adjective. Japanese uses two patterns, depending on the kind of adjective.

examples.text: 友達の話は面白かったです。
その話は面白かったです。
この部屋は静かでした。

contrasts.says: Verbs use -ました. An い adjective instead uses -かったです.
面白い changes its own ending; 静か keeps its form and uses でした.

mistakes.wrong: 友達の話は面白いでした。
mistakes.right: 友達の話は面白かったです。
mistakes.why: Do not put でした after the unchanged い adjective. Make the adjective past with かった.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 41–60, open to correction.

to-omou.explain: Put what you think before と, then finish with 思います. Use a verb’s dictionary form inside the thought: 来ます becomes 来る, 帰ります becomes 帰る, and 始まります becomes 始まる. 友達は五時に来ると思います means I think my friend will come at five. An い adjective needs no です before と: この映画は面白いと思います. This round uses only these affirmative nonpast thoughts. Noun and な-adjective thoughts, and the other plain forms, come later. Time and place keep their own particles; time before place is useful but not compulsory.
to-omou.why: English often starts with I think. Japanese saves 思います for the end, after the whole thought. A dictionary form inside it does not make the overall sentence casual.

examples.text: 映画は五時に始まると思います。
examples.means: I think the film starts at five.
examples.literal: Film five o'clock at starts think.

examples.text: 母はここに来ると思います。
examples.means: I think Mom will come here.

examples.text: 姉は五時に帰ると思います。
examples.means: I think my older sister will go home at five.
examples.literal: Older sister five o'clock at goes home think.

contrasts.says: 来ます is a polite verb ending on its own. Before と思います, this lesson uses 来る.
The と after a thought marks what you think. The と after a person can mean with.

mistakes.wrong: 母はここに来ると思うます。
mistakes.right: 母はここに来ると思います。
mistakes.why: 思う is the dictionary form. Its polite form is 思います, not the dictionary form with ます appended.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 41–60, open to correction.

kara-because.explain: Say the reason, add から, and then give the result: 電車が止まりましたから、遅れました. Keep the reason polite too: 時間がありますから or 忙しいですから. The ending before から still tells you whether that reason is present, past or negative. A comma can separate reason and result. This is different from から after a place or a time, which means from.
kara-because.why: English can put because and its reason after the result. These Japanese sentences put the reason first, with から at its end.

examples.text: 電車が止まりましたから、遅れました。
examples.means: I was late because the train stopped.

examples.text: 仕事がありますから、まだ会社にいます。
examples.means: I'm still at the office because I have work.
examples.literal: Work have because still office at am.

examples.text: お金がありませんから、家で食べます。
examples.means: I'll eat at home because I don't have any money.
examples.literal: Money don't have because home at eat.

contrasts.says: どうして asks why. A reason followed by から answers it.
から after a clause means because. After a time or a place it means from; that use is practiced next.

mistakes.wrong: お金があるませんから、家で食べます。
mistakes.right: お金がありませんから、家で食べます。
mistakes.why: The reason keeps its correct negative form, ありません, before から.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 41–60, open to correction.

verb-particles.explain: Learn the whole pairing: 友達を待ちます means wait for a friend; 友達に会います means meet a friend; 電車に乗ります means get on or ride a train; 家を出ます means leave home. In 家を出ます, を marks the place you leave. It does not mean the house is an object you act on. These particles stay the same in the past. 会います also allows と when describing a mutual meeting, so と is not a wrong alternative to に. Where an action happens can still take で: 駅で友達に会いました.
verb-particles.why: English prepositions do not map one for one to Japanese particles. English says wait for a friend but meet a friend with no preposition, while Japanese uses を for the first and に for the second.

examples.text: ここで友達を待っています。
examples.means: I'm waiting for my friend here.
examples.literal: Here at friend am waiting for.

examples.text: 五時に友達に会います。
examples.means: I'll meet my friend at five.

examples.text: この電車に乗ります。
五時に家を出ます。

contrasts.says: に can mark a destination, the person met, or a vehicle boarded. Learn its role with the verb.
を marks the person waited for and also the place left with 出ます.
友達と会います can describe a mutual meeting. It is valid, so it is not a distractor here.

mistakes.wrong: 友達に待っています。
mistakes.right: 友達を待っています。
mistakes.why: 待ちます takes を for the person you are waiting for.

mistakes.wrong: 友達を会います。
mistakes.right: 友達に会います。
mistakes.why: 会います does not take を for the person you meet.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 41–60, open to correction.

noun-modify.explain: Put the describing word before the noun. An い adjective needs no link: 面白い本 means interesting books, and 新しいペン means new pens. A な adjective takes な: 静かな部屋 means quiet rooms. きれい is a な adjective despite its final い, so use きれいな写真. Compare 部屋は静かです, a complete sentence, with 静かな部屋, a noun phrase. Do not keep です inside the noun phrase. The usual particles and counters then follow: 面白い本が二冊あります.
noun-modify.why: Both languages put these descriptions before nouns. Japanese also distinguishes the two adjective classes: only a な adjective takes な.

examples.text: 面白い本が二冊あります。
静かな部屋が二つあります。
きれいな写真が二枚あります。

contrasts.says: 部屋は静かです describes the room in a sentence. 静かな部屋 puts quiet inside the noun phrase.
母の本 links two nouns with の. 面白い本 uses an い adjective directly; 静かな部屋 uses a な adjective with な.

mistakes.wrong: 面白いです本が二冊あります。
mistakes.right: 面白い本が二冊あります。
mistakes.why: Do not carry the polite sentence ending です into a noun phrase. 面白い goes directly before 本.

mistakes.wrong: 静かです部屋が二つあります。
mistakes.right: 静かな部屋が二つあります。
mistakes.why: Before 部屋, 静か takes な, not the sentence ending です.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 61–80, open to correction.

naide-kudasai.explain: To ask someone not to do something, put the verb in its ない form and add でください. 置く becomes 置かない: 本をそこに置かないでください means please do not put the book there. 開ける drops る before ない: このドアを開けないでください means please do not open this door. These examples introduce the ない form within polite requests; using it as a casual sentence ending comes later. Keep the same particles for the thing and place. ません is the polite negative ending, but it cannot go directly before ください.
naide-kudasai.why: English adds do not after please. Japanese changes the verb to its negative form and uses でください after it.

examples.text: 本をそこに置かないでください。
examples.means: Please don't put the book there.

examples.text: このドアを開けないでください。
まだドアを開けないでください。
examples.means: Please don't open the door yet.

contrasts.says: 置いてください asks someone to put something down. 置かないでください asks them not to.
置きません says I will not put it there. 置かないでください asks someone else not to put it there.

mistakes.wrong: 本をそこに置きませんください。
mistakes.right: 本をそこに置かないでください。
mistakes.why: A negative request uses 置かないで before ください, not the polite negative 置きません.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 61–80, open to correction.

purpose.explain: Say why someone goes, comes or returns with a verb stem plus に: 飲みます loses ます to become 飲み, so お茶を飲みに行きます means go to drink tea. 会います gives 会い: 兄に会いに行きます means go to meet my older brother. The first に marks the person met; the second marks the purpose. The last verb carries politeness, and can be 行きます, 来ます, 帰ります or an invitation such as 行きましょう. An activity noun also works: 散歩に行きます means go for a walk. This is a purpose construction with movement; it is not a general translation of every English to plus verb.
purpose.why: English says go to drink or come to meet. Japanese puts the intended activity first, then に and the motion verb.

examples.text: お茶を飲みに行きます。
examples.means: I'm going to have some tea.

examples.text: 兄に会いに行きます。
examples.means: I'm going to see my older brother.

examples.text: 母に会いに帰ります。
examples.means: I'm going home to see Mom.

examples.text: この公園は安全です。散歩に行きましょう。
examples.means: This park is safe. Let's go for a walk.
examples.literal: This park safe is. A walk for let's go.

contrasts.says: 学校に行きます gives a destination. 飲みに行きます gives the purpose of going.
兄に会いに行きます has two に particles: the person met after 兄, and the purpose after 会い.

mistakes.wrong: お茶を飲むに行きます。
mistakes.right: お茶を飲みに行きます。
mistakes.why: Purpose uses the ます stem 飲み, not the dictionary form 飲む.

mistakes.wrong: 兄に会うに行きます。
mistakes.right: 兄に会いに行きます。
mistakes.why: Use the stem 会い before the purpose に, not the dictionary form 会う.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 61–80, open to correction.

plain-form.explain: These lines are conversations between friends. 手伝う means help or will help, 手伝わない means do not or will not help, and 手伝った means helped. 行く, 行かない, 行った and 飲む, 飲まない, 飲んだ show two more sets. Learn the sets: the past is not made by simply attaching た to every dictionary form. The particles keep their jobs. 私が手伝う identifies the speaker as the person who will help. A name can identify the listener: 田中さんが行く？ asks a friend Tanaka whether they are the one going. Rising intonation asks the question here; it is written with ？. Polite speech remains the default with people you do not know well. This introduction practices verb forms; fuller plain-past practice comes later.
plain-form.why: English usually keeps the same verb when speaking to a friend or a stranger. Japanese commonly changes the ending. A plain verb inside a larger polite sentence does not make the whole sentence casual.

examples.text: 私が手伝う。
今日は手伝わない。
昨日、母を手伝った。
田中さんが行く？
examples.means: Are you the one going, Tanaka?

contrasts.says: 飲みます is polite. 飲む is plain; do not attach ます to 飲む.
The negative ない form already appeared in polite requests. Here 手伝わない ends a statement to a friend.
来る in 来ると思います belongs inside a thought. 行く in 田中さんが行く？ ends the casual question itself.

mistakes.wrong: 私が手伝うます。
mistakes.right: 私が手伝う。
mistakes.why: For this conversation with a friend, finish with the plain form 手伝う. A dictionary form cannot take ます directly.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 81–100, open to correction.

transitive-pairs.explain: 仕事の時間が変わりました reports that the working hours changed. 仕事の時間を変えます says someone will change them. The first verb, 変わる, describes a change in its subject; the second, 変える, takes the thing changed as its object. Likewise, 新しい仕事が始まります says the new job starts, while 新しい仕事を始めます says someone starts the job. A topic can still take は: 仕事は九時に始まります. The difference is in the verb and its roles, not a rule that every sentence must contain が or を. Learn the related verbs as pairs; there is no single ending that forms every pair. The later door lesson applies the same idea to a door opening and a person opening it.
transitive-pairs.why: English can use change or start for both roles. Japanese often chooses two different verbs, with the corresponding subject or object particle.

examples.text: 仕事の時間が変わりました。
仕事の時間を変えます。
新しい仕事を始めます。
仕事は九時に始まります。準備を始めましょう。
examples.means: Work starts at nine. Let's start getting ready.
examples.literal: Work nine o'clock at starts. Preparations let's start.

contrasts.says: 時間が変わります marks the hours as what changes.
時間を変えます marks the hours as what someone changes.

mistakes.wrong: 仕事の時間を変わりました。
mistakes.right: 仕事の時間が変わりました。
mistakes.why: 変わりました describes what changed. The hours are its subject, not an object.

mistakes.wrong: 新しい仕事を始まります。
mistakes.right: 新しい仕事を始めます。
mistakes.why: When someone starts the job marked with を, use 始めます.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 81–100, open to correction.

embedded-question.explain: An embedded question is the question you know the answer to, do not know the answer to, or ask someone to answer. 駅がどこにあるか分かりますか means do you know where the station is. The first か closes where the station is; the last か asks the listener whether they know. The inner verb is plain: ある for a thing, いる for a person, and 始まる for something starting. An い adjective also goes directly before か: どの答えが正しいか教えてください. For a noun question such as 予約は何時か分かりますか, put か after 何時, without です or だ. The whole sentence stays polite through 分かります, 分かりません, 知っています or 教えてください. These examples ask for a missing detail; questions meaning whether or not come later.
embedded-question.why: English says do you know where it is or please tell me which answer is correct. Japanese puts that entire inner question before か and then gives the knowing or telling part.

examples.text: 駅がどこにあるか分かりますか。
examples.means: Do you know where the station is?

examples.text: かばんがどこにあるか分かりません。
examples.means: I don't know where the bag is.

examples.text: 予約は何時か分かりますか。
examples.means: Do you know what time the appointment is?

examples.text: どの答えが正しいか教えてください。
examples.means: Please tell me which answer is correct.

contrasts.says: A final か asks the whole question. The first か in 駅がどこにあるか分かりますか instead closes the question about location.
ある and いる are plain inside these questions, but the outer endings remain polite.

mistakes.wrong: 学校がどこにあるを教えてください。
mistakes.right: 学校がどこにあるか教えてください。
mistakes.why: Do not treat the bare question clause as a noun followed by を. Mark the embedded question with か. A complete embedded question can also take を after か; that is not this mistake.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 81–100, open to correction.

yo-ne.explain: よ and ね follow a complete sentence ending. 今、少し話せますよ offers information or reassurance that the speaker can talk. 今は時間がありますよ reassures someone that there is time. ね looks for shared understanding: 一分だけですね confirms just one minute, and 今週は忙しいですね shares the impression of a busy week. After an intended action, 明日、電話しますね gently confirms the plan to call tomorrow. The English okay or right is sometimes helpful, but ね does not always ask for a spoken answer. Both particles work with polite endings; this lesson keeps です and ます. よ and ね are not grammatical opposites: replacing one with the other can make a different, perfectly valid sentence. Use the situation and tone to choose.
yo-ne.why: English often expresses this relationship to the listener through intonation, a tag such as right, or a reassuring phrase. Japanese can make it explicit with a final particle.

examples.text: 今、少し話せますよ。
examples.means: I can talk for a little while now.

examples.text: 一分だけですね。
明日、電話しますね。
今週は忙しいですね。
examples.means: It's a busy week, isn't it?

contrasts.says: か directly marks a question. ね can invite agreement or acknowledge a shared situation without directly asking a question.
よ and ね come after the correct ending: 電話しますね keeps the polite 電話します.

mistakes.wrong: 明日、電話するますね。
mistakes.right: 明日、電話しますね。
mistakes.why: Keep the correctly formed polite verb before ね. The plain dictionary form cannot take ます directly.

mistakes.wrong: 一分だけだですね。
mistakes.right: 一分だけですね。
mistakes.why: Use the polite copula です before ね. Do not combine plain だ and polite です.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 81–100, open to correction.

tsumori.explain: つもりです states an intention or plan. Put the verb in its dictionary form: 行くつもりです, 休むつもりです, するつもりです. To state an intention not to do something, put the negative plain form before つもり: 行かないつもりです or 飲まないつもりです. Keep です at the end when speaking politely. A plan is not a guarantee; つもり describes the intention. These examples chiefly state the speaker's own plans. A question can ask about the listener's intention. Do not put ます between the verb and つもり.
tsumori.why: English puts intend or plan before the action. Japanese puts つもり after the plain verb and saves です for the end. A plain verb inside this construction does not make the conversation casual.

examples.text: 明日は公園に行くつもりです。
examples.means: I plan to go to the park tomorrow.

examples.text: 明日は家で休むつもりです。
examples.means: I plan to rest at home tomorrow.

examples.text: 今晩はコーヒーを飲まないつもりです。
examples.means: I intend not to drink coffee tonight.

contrasts.says: 行きます can state a future action. 行くつもりです explicitly states an intention.
Use the dictionary or negative plain form before つもり, while the outer sentence ends politely in です.

mistakes.wrong: 明日は公園に行きますつもりです。
mistakes.right: 明日は公園に行くつもりです。
mistakes.why: Use the plain 行く before つもり, not the polite 行きます.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 101–120, open to correction.

tara.explain: Use the verb's plain past form and add ら: ある gives あったら, 終わる gives 終わったら, and 困る gives 困ったら. Put the condition before the action or request. 時間があったら、手伝ってください asks for help if the listener has time. 仕事が終わったら、電話してください asks for a call once work is finished. Although the form contains the past ending, these conditions look ahead; they do not say that the event has already happened. If or when depends on the situation: a possibility versus an event expected to finish. This lesson practices affirmative verb conditions, with a polite main clause.
tara.why: English puts if or when before a clause. Japanese puts the conditional ending on the verb at the end of that clause. The request can still use ください or a polite can-question.

examples.text: 時間があったら、手伝ってください。
examples.means: Please help me if you have time.

examples.text: 仕事が終わったら、電話してください。
examples.means: Please call me when work is finished.

examples.text: 困ったら、先生に聞いてください。
examples.means: Please ask the teacher if you have trouble.
examples.literal: if have trouble teacher ask please.

contrasts.says: The plain past supplies the form, but adding ら makes it a condition, not a completed-past statement.
から gives a reason treated as true. たら sets a condition for what follows.

mistakes.wrong: 時間があるたら、手伝ってください。
mistakes.right: 時間があったら、手伝ってください。
mistakes.why: Use あった, the past form of ある, plus ら: あったら. Do not attach たら to the dictionary form.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 101–120, open to correction.

morau.explain: もらいます looks at a gift from the receiver's side. In 母に小説をもらいました, the understood receiver is I, 母に identifies Mom as the giver, and 小説を is the thing received. から can also mark the giver, so it is not a wrong substitute for に. Compare 友達が小説をくれました: now the friend is the subject and gives the novel to me. With あげます, someone gives to someone else: 妹にあげます says I will give it to my younger sister. The role of に depends on the verb: giver with もらう, receiver with あげる or くれる. Keep ます or ました in these polite sentences. This lesson is about receiving things; receiving someone's help with てもらう comes later.
morau.why: English changes the viewpoint with give and receive too. Japanese also distinguishes giving toward the speaker or the speaker's group with くれる. Work out who gives, who receives and which verb is being used.

examples.text: 母に小説をもらいました。
examples.means: I received a novel from Mom.

examples.text: 友達にこの本をもらいます。
examples.means: I'll receive this book from a friend.
examples.literal: friend from this book will receive.

examples.text: 友達が小説をくれました。
examples.means: A friend gave me a novel.

contrasts.says: 友達が小説をくれました takes the giver as subject. 母に小説をもらいました takes the understood receiver as subject.
に marks different roles with different verbs: 母にもらいます receives from Mom; 妹にあげます gives to a younger sister.

mistakes.wrong: 友達にこの本をもらうます。
mistakes.right: 友達にこの本をもらいます。
mistakes.why: もらう is the dictionary form. The polite form is もらいます; do not add ます directly to もらう.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 101–120, open to correction.

ta-form.explain: The plain past can finish a statement or question to a friend. 見る becomes 見た, 逃げる becomes 逃げた, and 捕まえる becomes 捕まえた: these verbs drop る and add た. This is not the pattern for every verb ending in る. You already met 手伝った, 行った and 飲んだ; learn each verb's form rather than adding た to its dictionary form. The particles keep their usual roles: 警察官が犯人を捕まえた. A rising voice, written ？ here, asks この映画を見た？ The film lesson is explicitly a conversation between friends. With a stranger, keep a polite ending such as 見ました. This lesson expands affirmative past practice; it does not introduce plain negative past or the experience pattern たことがある.
ta-form.why: English usually keeps the same past verb regardless of the listener. Japanese distinguishes the polite 見ました from the plain 見た. Both can report a past event; the relationship determines the register.

examples.text: 昨日、怖い映画を見た。
examples.means: I watched a scary film yesterday.

examples.text: 犯人が逃げた。
警察官が犯人を捕まえた。
examples.means: A police officer caught the culprit.

examples.text: この映画を見た？

contrasts.says: This expands the earlier introduction of 手伝った, 行った and 飲んだ into a whole film conversation.
見ました is polite past. 見た is plain past; choose the ending for the listener.
たら uses the plain past shape plus ら for a condition. A standalone 見た reports a past event instead.

mistakes.wrong: この映画を見るます？
mistakes.right: この映画を見た？
mistakes.why: For this past question to a friend, use 見た. 見るます is not a conjugation; a dictionary form cannot take ます directly.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 101–120, open to correction.

koto.explain: こと turns an action or fact into something you can talk about as a noun. Keep the verb and its object together: 本を読むこと is the activity of reading books. 本を読むことが好きです says I like that activity. With は, you can describe the action: 小説を書くことは難しいです. メモを書くことはできます says that writing a note is something I can do. These examples use the dictionary form before こと, while the outer sentence stays polite. Do not add な or の between this verb and こと. 好き is a な adjective, not a verb: 好きです is like, and 好きじゃないです is do not like. こと has other uses, but this lesson practices activities. The experience pattern with a past verb comes later in this round.
koto.why: English often uses an -ing phrase or an infinitive as a subject or object. Japanese keeps its plain verb and adds こと, then the particle needed by the outer sentence.

examples.text: この説明を理解することは難しいです。
examples.literal: this explanation understand the act of difficult is.

examples.text: 本を読むことが好きです。
examples.literal: books read the act of liked is.

examples.text: 小説を書くことは難しいです。
examples.literal: novel write the act of difficult is.

contrasts.says: The verb inside the group is plain even when the whole sentence ends politely.
A な adjective uses な before a noun; a verb before こと does not.

mistakes.wrong: 本を読むなことが好きです。
mistakes.right: 本を読むことが好きです。
mistakes.why: 読む is a verb. Link it directly to こと: 読むこと, without な.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 121–140, open to correction.

toki.explain: とき places one action in the time of another situation. Put the situation before it, then give the main action: 家にいるとき、音楽を聞きます. Verbs use a plain form, い adjectives attach directly, な adjectives take な, and nouns take の: いるとき, 忙しいとき, 静かなとき, 休みのとき. A は after とき can make the time setting the topic. The main verb still gives politeness and its own tense. A dictionary form can show an action not yet completed at that point: 家に帰るとき、駅でパンを買います means buying bread on the way home. A past form can show the action as completed: 家に帰ったとき、母に会いました means meeting Mom on getting home. This difference is about the relation between the two events, not simply English present versus past. The lesson uses these affirmative patterns; it does not teach every possible tense combination.
toki.why: English usually puts when before a clause. Japanese puts とき after it. Decide what situation holds, or what action has been completed, at the time of the main action.

examples.text: 家にいるとき、音楽を聞きます。
examples.means: I listen to music when I'm at home.
examples.literal: home at am when music listen to.

examples.text: 休みのとき、子供と公園に行きます。
examples.means: I go to the park with my child when I'm off work.
examples.literal: day off when child with park to go.

examples.text: 家に帰るとき、駅でパンを買います。
examples.means: I buy bread at the station on my way home.
examples.literal: home to return when station at bread buy.

examples.text: 家に帰ったとき、母に会いました。
examples.means: I saw Mom when I got home.
examples.literal: home to returned when Mom met.

contrasts.says: たら sets a condition or an event after which something follows; とき gives a time setting. Their uses overlap, but they are not interchangeable everywhere.
The links before とき follow the same adjective distinction: 忙しいとき but 静かなとき.

mistakes.wrong: 家にいるのとき、音楽を聞きます。
mistakes.right: 家にいるとき、音楽を聞きます。
mistakes.why: いる is a verb, so it attaches directly to とき. The の link belongs after a noun such as 休み.

mistakes.wrong: 忙しいなとき、家族に頼みます。
mistakes.right: 忙しいとき、家族に頼みます。
mistakes.why: 忙しい is an い adjective. Do not insert な before とき.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 121–140, open to correction.

relative-clause.explain: Put the clause that identifies a person or thing immediately before its noun. 昨日会った人 means the person I met yesterday: 会った is plain past and 人 is the person met. あそこにいる人 means the person who is over there: the noun is now the person doing the being. Japanese adds no separate word for who or that. Do not repeat that person inside the describing clause. If another person is the subject inside, use が: 私が会った人 is the person I met. The whole noun group then takes the particle needed in the main sentence. In 昨日会った人の顔を覚えていますか, の connects that person to their face, and を marks the face remembered. There is no の between 会った and 人. These lessons use plain verb forms in noun modifiers, with polite main clauses. Formal Japanese can also use certain polite modifiers; those are not used as wrong answers here.
relative-clause.why: English usually puts who or that and the description after the noun. Japanese puts the description first, so wait for the noun before deciding what the whole group identifies.

examples.text: 昨日会った人の顔を覚えていますか。
examples.means: Do you remember the face of the person you met yesterday?

examples.text: あそこにいる人を知っていますか。
examples.means: Do you know the person over there?
examples.literal: over there at is person know.

examples.text: 私が会った人は先生です。
examples.means: The person I met is a teacher.

contrasts.says: An adjective and a whole clause both precede the noun they describe.
の links nouns, as in 人の顔. A verb directly describing 人 does not take の: 会った人.

mistakes.wrong: 昨日会ったの人の顔を覚えていますか。
mistakes.right: 昨日会った人の顔を覚えていますか。
mistakes.why: 会った directly describes 人. Do not insert the noun-linking の between this verb and its noun.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 121–140, open to correction.

nagara.explain: For two activities by the same person at the same time, put ながら after the first verb stem. 聞きます becomes 聞きながら, 飲みます becomes 飲みながら, and 読みます becomes 読みながら. コーヒーを飲みながら小説を読んでいます makes reading the main activity and drinking coffee the accompanying one. Both actions belong to the same person. The last verb carries tense and politeness, so ながら itself does not change. Keep objects and other particles with the actions they belong to. 座って can describe the posture maintained during an activity: いすに座って、音楽を聞きながら本を読んでいます. To stay seated through an activity, 座って is the usual choice, as in the example. This lesson teaches simultaneous actions, not the contrasting use of ながら.
nagara.why: English can put while before a whole clause. This Japanese pattern attaches to a verb stem and shares one doer between its two actions.

examples.text: いすに座って、音楽を聞きながら本を読んでいます。
examples.means: I'm sitting in a chair reading a book while listening to music.
examples.literal: chair in sitting music listen while book am reading.

examples.text: コーヒーを飲みながら小説を読んでいます。
examples.means: I'm reading a novel while drinking coffee.
examples.literal: coffee drink while novel am reading.

examples.text: 説明を読みながらパソコンを使います。
examples.means: I use the computer while reading the instructions.

contrasts.says: A て link can join actions or maintain a posture. ながら explicitly says that two activities overlap.
The main verb may end in ています to say the combined activities are happening now.

mistakes.wrong: コーヒーを飲むながら小説を読んでいます。
mistakes.right: コーヒーを飲みながら小説を読んでいます。
mistakes.why: Use the stem 飲み before ながら, not the dictionary form 飲む.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 121–140, open to correction.

ta-koto-ga-aru.explain: A plain past verb plus ことがある describes previous experience. Use polite あります in these lessons: この店で食べたことがあります means I have eaten at this restaurant before. A question adds か; ことがありません says there is no such experience. Keep the past form even for no experience: この料理は食べたことがありません. A は can replace が to make the experience the topic, as in 家でパンを作ったことはありますか. The pattern does not name a particular completed occasion; it says the experience exists. An already-completed meal on a particular occasion uses an ordinary past with もう, not this experience pattern. Learn the past forms: 食べた, 作った, 来た, 飲んだ. The た ending describes the experienced action, while あります locates that experience in the present.
ta-koto-ga-aru.why: English have done can refer either to experience or to a recent completed event. Japanese makes the experience meaning explicit with ことがあります.

examples.text: この店で食べたことがあります。
examples.means: I've eaten at this restaurant before.
examples.literal: this restaurant at ate experience there is.

examples.text: この料理を食べたことがありますか。
examples.means: Have you ever eaten this dish?
examples.literal: this dish ate experience there is.

examples.text: この料理は食べたことがありません。
examples.literal: this dish ate experience there is not.

examples.text: 家でパンを作ったことはありますか。
examples.means: Have you ever made bread at home?
examples.literal: home at bread made experience there is.

contrasts.says: こと first turned an activity into a noun-like group. Here the past verb and あります together make the specific experience construction.
An ordinary polite past reports an event. たことがあります says that someone has had the experience before.

mistakes.wrong: この料理を食べたのことがありますか。
mistakes.right: この料理を食べたことがありますか。
mistakes.why: The plain past attaches directly to こと. Do not insert の between 食べた and こと.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 121–140, open to correction.

must.explain: なければなりません expresses a requirement or necessity. Start from the negative verb and replace its final ない with なければ: 開けなければ, 押さなければ, 使わなければ. Add なりません to complete the expression. Its two negative parts work together: not doing the action will not do, so the action is necessary. The whole sentence stays polite. This is an everyday correct form, though more formal than the shortened forms used between close friends. This lesson teaches it as a complete expression; broader uses of conditional ば come later. The lesson's title, We got the door open, is 開けられました: the familiar potential, reporting that opening the door succeeded, not an obligation in the past.
must.why: English have to is affirmative. Japanese expresses the requirement through a negative condition and a negative result; do not read it as must not.

examples.text: このドアを開けなければなりません。
examples.means: We have to open this door.
examples.literal: this door if do not open will not do.

examples.text: ドアを少し押さなければなりません。
examples.means: We have to push the door a little.
examples.literal: door a little if do not push will not do.

examples.text: この鍵を使わなければなりません。
examples.means: We have to use this key.
examples.literal: this key if do not use will not do.

contrasts.says: 開けられました reports that opening succeeded. 開けなければなりません says opening is necessary.
なりません is negative, but the complete double-negative expression requires the action.

mistakes.wrong: このドアを開けないなりません。
mistakes.right: このドアを開けなければなりません。
mistakes.why: Change the negative ending ない to なければ before なりません: 開けなければなりません.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 141–160, open to correction.

passive.explain: The passive focuses on the thing receiving an action. 作る gives 作られる, 使う gives 使われる, and 読む gives 読まれる: these verbs change to the a-row sound and add れる, with う becoming わ. Add polite endings in the usual way. 作られています can describe something being made now or a regular manufacturing activity. 読まれています can describe a book still being read by people generally. 作られました reports that something was made. A doer can be left unsaid when it is not the point. Do not simply switch が and を on the active verb: the verb must change too. Other verbs use られる, which can also mark ability; context determines the meaning. These examples focus on objects and ordinary passive descriptions, not respectful speech or the indirect passive.
passive.why: English uses be plus a past participle. Japanese changes the verb itself, then adds the appropriate tense and politeness ending.

examples.text: 今、新しいソファが作られています。
examples.means: A new sofa is being made now.
examples.literal: now new sofa is being made.

examples.text: このテーブルは昔作られました。
examples.means: This table was made a long time ago.
examples.literal: this table long ago was made.

examples.text: この部屋は会議に使われます。
examples.means: This room is used for meetings.
examples.literal: this room meetings for is used.

examples.text: この小説は今も読まれています。
examples.means: This novel is still read today.
examples.literal: this novel now too is read.

contrasts.says: An intransitive verb says something happens; a passive presents it as receiving an action.
Some passive and potential forms look alike. The subject and the situation establish the intended reading.

mistakes.wrong: この町でいすが作られります。
mistakes.right: この町でいすが作られます。
mistakes.why: The passive 作られる conjugates like an ichidan verb: 作られます. Do not insert り before ます.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 141–160, open to correction.

superlative.explain: 一番 selects the highest degree within a group understood from the situation. While viewing houses, この家が一番広いです identifies this house as the most spacious among the choices. 一番好き says like best. No special adjective ending is added: 広い and 明るい stay as they are. When the description comes before a noun, the usual adjective link still applies: 一番静かな家. The が in どの部屋が一番明るいですか asks which room has that highest degree. The group need not be stated if everyone knows the available choices. This does not claim that the house is the largest in the world.
superlative.why: English often changes the adjective to -est or adds most. Japanese keeps the adjective and puts 一番 before it.

examples.text: この家が一番広いです。
examples.means: This house is the most spacious.

examples.text: どの部屋が一番明るいですか。
一番静かな家に住みたいです。
examples.means: I want to live in the quietest house.
examples.literal: most quiet house in want to live.

examples.text: この家が一番好きです。

contrasts.says: Keep な after a な adjective before a noun: 一番静かな家. An い adjective links directly.
一番 changes the degree, not the adjective conjugation.

mistakes.wrong: 一番静かです家に住みたいです。
mistakes.right: 一番静かな家に住みたいです。
mistakes.why: 静か needs な before 家. です ends a statement; it does not link this adjective to the noun.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 141–160, open to correction.

comparison.explain: より follows the standard of comparison: この家は友達の家より広いです says this house is more spacious than my friend's. The adjective stays unchanged. Noun plus のほうが singles out one alternative: この部屋のほうが明るいです. With いい or 好き, the construction can express a preference. The other alternative can be stated with より or understood from the situation. 私はコーヒーよりお茶が好きです prefers tea to coffee. もっと asks for or describes a greater degree or amount, as in もっとゆっくり and もっと時間. Later practice can put a plain verb directly before ほう: unlike a noun, that verb needs no の. Do not insert a preposition-like に between a noun and ほう.
comparison.why: Japanese names the comparison standard before より. English usually places than after the comparative adjective, so the ordering differs.

examples.text: この家は友達の家より広いです。
examples.means: This house is more spacious than my friend's house.
examples.literal: this house friend 's house than spacious is.

examples.text: この部屋のほうが明るいです。
examples.means: This room is the brighter one.

examples.text: ソファよりいすのほうがいいです。
examples.means: I'd rather have a chair than a sofa.
examples.literal: sofa than chair 's side good is.

examples.text: もっとゆっくり話してください。

contrasts.says: 一番 selects the top degree in a group; より compares against a particular standard.
Use の between a noun and ほう, even though English does not translate it as possession here.

mistakes.wrong: この部屋にほうが明るいです。
mistakes.right: この部屋のほうが明るいです。
mistakes.why: 部屋 is a noun. Link it to ほう with の: 部屋のほう, not 部屋にほう.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 141–160, open to correction.

te-ageru.explain: The て form joins an action to a giving or receiving verb. あげます describes doing something for someone else; くれます describes someone doing it for me or my group. てもらいます presents the subject as receiving someone's help, often the speaker but not always: 先生に計画を説明してもらいました. With もらいます, に marks the helper, not the receiver. In 姉が私の話を聞いてくれます, 姉 is the person who kindly listens. The last verb carries tense and politeness. てくれませんか is a polite request, not an accusation that someone refuses; てくれますか also asks for help. あげます can sound patronizing if you announce your own favor directly to an adult recipient, so these examples describe help to a third person or care for a child. Do not use the dictionary form or ます form in place of the joining て form.
te-ageru.why: English may use for me, have someone do it, or simply describe the helpful action. Japanese explicitly marks its direction and whose viewpoint is taken.

examples.text: この計画を説明してくれませんか。
examples.means: Could you explain this plan to me?
examples.literal: this plan explain would you do for me.

examples.text: 友達が計画を説明してくれました。
examples.means: A friend explained the plan to me.
examples.literal: friend plan explain did for me.

examples.text: 先生に計画を説明してもらいました。
examples.means: I had the teacher explain the plan to me.
examples.literal: teacher from plan explain received the help.

examples.text: 私が妹に本を読んであげます。
examples.means: I'll read a book to my younger sister.
examples.literal: I younger sister for book read will do as a favor.

contrasts.says: もらいます first described receiving a thing. After a て verb, it describes receiving help with that action.
てください requests an action directly. てくれませんか asks someone to do it for you.

mistakes.wrong: この計画を説明するくれませんか。
mistakes.right: この計画を説明してくれませんか。
mistakes.why: Use 説明して, the て form, to connect the action to くれる.

mistakes.wrong: 先生を計画を説明してもらいました。
mistakes.right: 先生に計画を説明してもらいました。
mistakes.why: With てもらう, に marks the person whose help is received. を already marks the plan being explained.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 141–160, open to correction.

ba-to.explain: ば gives a condition. For a godan verb, change its final u-row sound to the e-row sound and add ば: ある becomes あれば. A negative ending ない changes to なければ: 見えなければ. This lesson uses states such as having time or not being able to see, so a request or suggestion can naturally follow. Plain nonpast plus と gives a predictable or recurring result: 急ぐと転びます. The result clause keeps its polite ending. Do not use this result と as a general way to introduce your request or intention; use the familiar たら or an appropriate ば condition. The same written と also joins companions or introduces thoughts, so read its role from the clause.
ba-to.why: English if can cover several relationships. Japanese distinguishes a stated condition with ば from an expected consequence with と.

examples.text: 急ぐと、転びます。気をつけてください。
examples.means: If you rush, you'll fall. Please be careful.
examples.literal: hurry if will fall be careful please.

examples.text: 段差があれば、気をつけてください。
examples.means: If there's a step, please be careful.
examples.literal: step if there is be careful please.

examples.text: 足元が見えなければ、ここで止まってください。
examples.means: If you can't see the ground at your feet, please stop here.
examples.literal: ground at your feet if cannot see here at stop please.

examples.text: 時間があれば、ゆっくり歩きましょう。
examples.means: If we have time, let's walk at a leisurely pace.
examples.literal: time if there is leisurely let's walk.

contrasts.says: たら remains useful for a request after an event is completed. These ば examples instead set a state as the condition.
The なければ in the necessity expression is the same negative conditional shape. Here its result can be a different clause.

mistakes.wrong: 時間があるば、ゆっくり歩きましょう。
mistakes.right: 時間があれば、ゆっくり歩きましょう。
mistakes.why: ある becomes あれば. Do not attach ば directly to the dictionary form.

mistakes.wrong: 急ぐば、転びます。気をつけてください。
mistakes.right: 急ぐと、転びます。気をつけてください。
mistakes.why: For this predictable result use plain 急ぐ plus と. A ば condition would need the conjugated form 急げば.

source.note: Written with the Japanese lessons 141–160, open to correction.
